query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor tungsten doping (~0.5–1 at.%) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a stable, adaptive lubricious tribolayer during sliding, leading to a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate over the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard, homogeneous CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a single-phase (FCC) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with a small addition of tungsten during processing.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribology tests in atmospheric air under variable normal loads and sliding speeds with test temperatures ranging from approximately room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a surface-enriched, tungsten-assisted lubricious phase (such as an oxide or nanoprecipitate layer) that adapts and remains stable throughout the tested temperature range.
generation.mechanism: Tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and promotes surface segregation under sliding. At lower temperatures, this accelerates microstructural refinement and lowers shear strength, while at higher temperatures, tungsten facilitates the formation of a protective lubricious phase that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the tungsten-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a consistently lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The CoCrFeNi alloy without tungsten doping, which typically shows higher friction and wear, especially at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention is anticipated under controlled laboratory conditions (atmospheric air, moderate loads, and sliding speeds). Its performance beyond these conditions (e.g., in non-oxidizing environments or under extreme loads) remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of friction and wear improvements, as well as the detailed characteristics of the lubricious tribolayer, may vary with experimental parameters and require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set with the tungsten doping (0.5–1 at.%) and one undoped (baseline). Conduct systematic ball-on-disk sliding tests under identical conditions (controlled normal loads, sliding speeds, and a temperature ramp from room temperature to 800 °C) in atmospheric air. Use real-time friction measurements and post-test surface analyses.
measurements: Steady-state coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear track dimensions and specific wear rate (mm³/N·m)
Surface composition and morphology (using techniques such as SEM/EDS or XPS) to detect the formation and stability of the lubricious tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant and reproducible reduction in the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the baseline across the full temperature range, or if surface analyses fail to confirm the formation of a stable adaptive tribolayer, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 3A shows the Vickers hardness and wear rate variations of NiX and Ni3X as the temperature increases from RT to 800 °C. The hardness of NiX and Ni3X gradually decreases from 6.1 GPa and 4.3 GPa at RT to 3.7 GPa and 2.5 GPa at 800 °C, respectively. The high thermal hardness of NiX arises from the solid solution strengthening and the resultant heterostructures [,]. The trend in wear rate of the Ni3X with temperature is similar to that of the conventional alloys. Specifically, its wear rate increases from 1.1 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at RT to 4.2 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 600 °C, but decreases afterward to 2.4 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 800 °C. However, the wear rate of the NiX is basically maintained at the order of (10−7 to 10−6) mm3/Nm over the entire test temperature. In particular, it achieves ultra-low wear at RT (1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm) and 800 °C (9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm). drafts.hypothesis: Adding a carefully chosen microalloying element that forms an in‐situ lubricious phase during sliding will enable the CoCrFeNi alloy to maintain low friction and wear across the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C).
drafts.material_initial_state: Standard CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its typical solid-solution microstructure.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a single alloying addition designed to produce a continuous lubricious tribofilm during wear. This alloying element should be selected so that it remains inert at lower temperatures and forms a lubricating oxide or similar phase at higher temperatures.
drafts.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed under a constant load in a controlled atmospheric environment, with temperature varied from room temperature up to 800 °C.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, in-situ lubricious tribofilm at the sliding surface, mediated by the microalloying element, which adapts its chemistry (e.g., oxidation state) as temperature increases.
drafts.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the microalloying addition promotes the dispersion of secondary phases that reduce direct metal contact. As the temperature increases, the element reacts with ambient species (e.g., oxygen) to form a lubricious oxide (or a similar low-shear phase) that maintains a protective, low-friction interface. This dual behavior provides a smart, temperature-adaptive lubrication effect.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate uniformly from room temperature to 800 °C due to the persistent lubricious tribofilm.
drafts.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which typically shows degradation in friction and wear performance at higher temperatures.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under sliding conditions at temperatures from ambient up to 800 °C, under a fixed load and in a controlled atmospheric environment. Its performance may not extend beyond these specific operational windows (e.g., at much higher temperatures or under different environmental conditions such as varying oxidizing conditions).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of experimental samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloys and one set modified with the selected microalloying addition. Conduct sliding wear tests at room temperature, an intermediate temperature (e.g., 400 °C), and 800 °C under identical loads and controlled atmospheric conditions. Use surface analytical techniques (e.g., XPS, SEM, and EDS) to examine the formation and continuity of the lubricious tribofilm.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across the temperature range
Wear rate under identical loading conditions
Surface composition and morphology (to confirm the presence of the in-situ lubricious tribofilm)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvement in friction and wear performance compared to the baseline at all tested temperatures, or if surface analyses fail to reveal a continuous lubricious tribofilm that correlates with the improved tribological behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor concentration of a selected trace element that segregates to the alloy surface during sliding and forms a stable, self-lubricating second phase will lower the friction coefficient and wear rate of a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy over a broad temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with its standard homogeneous microstructure and known sliding tribological performance.
drafts.intervention: Alloying the CoCrFeNi matrix with a trace element (identity not presupposed) that is capable of in situ segregation and formation of a lubricious phase during sliding.
drafts.conditions: Sliding tribology tests performed in atmospheric air under variable load conditions and over a temperature range from approximately 25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C.
drafts.structural_mediator: An in situ formed, surface-enriched lubricious phase (e.g., an oxide or alternative metallic compound) that remains stable over the full temperature span.
drafts.mechanism: During sliding, the trace element segregates to the surface. At elevated temperatures, its oxidation or transformation produces a lubricious phase that acts as a stable tribolayer, reducing metal-to-metal contact. At lower temperatures, the presence of the dopant may also refine surface microstructure and improve contact behavior, thus lowering both friction and wear.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting CoCrFeNi alloy, the doped alloy is expected to show consistently lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates across the entire temperature range (25–800 °C).
drafts.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which is known to experience higher friction and wear, with improvements in other systems reported only up to around 704 °C.
drafts.boundary: Effectiveness is expected within the controlled laboratory environment: atmospheric air, variable loads mimicking application conditions, and a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C. The intervention’s performance outside these conditions or under extreme, untested environmental factors remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy specimens and another set doped with the chosen concentration of the trace element. Conduct sliding tribology tests under identical environmental conditions and controlled loads, gradually varying the temperature from 25 °C to 800 °C. Use both in situ friction/wear measurements and post-test surface analysis.
measurements: Wear scar dimensions and volume loss measurements
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS or SEM-EDS) to confirm presence and stability of the lubricious phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy does not demonstrate significantly reduced friction and wear over the full temperature range compared to the baseline or if surface analyses fail to reveal the formation of a stable, self-lubricating tribolayer, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small fraction of tungsten (W) as a dopant into the CoCrFeNi alloy will promote the in situ formation of a stable, adaptive tribolayer that mitigates friction and wear across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: A single-phase, FCC CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) with relatively soft, coarse-grained microstructure typical of the as-processed state.
drafts.intervention: Introduce ~0.5 atomic percent tungsten into the CoCrFeNi matrix by alloying (e.g., via modified powder metallurgy or melting route), thereby altering the alloy’s composition and microstructure.
drafts.conditions: Dry sliding tests under variable loads and sliding speeds in air, covering temperatures from room temperature (RT) up to 800 °C, where oxidation and grain refinement effects are critical.
drafts.structural_mediator: The tungsten addition is expected to induce increased lattice distortion and promote the formation of fine, W-induced nanoprecipitates and refined grain boundary structures that serve as nucleation sites for a protective, reactive wear film.
drafts.mechanism: W incorporation enhances high-temperature stability by delaying the fracture of nascent oxide or amorphous tribolayers, while also facilitating dynamic grain refinement at the frictional interface. Together, these effects foster a self-organized adaptive tribolayer that maintains a low shear strength and stable friction coefficient under varying temperature and load conditions.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the undoped alloy, the W-doped CoCrFeNi alloy will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced specific wear rates across the entire temperature interval from RT to 800 °C.
drafts.baseline: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy shows good wear resistance under certain conditions but struggles to maintain low friction and minimal wear across the full temperature range due to temperature-sensitive mechanisms such as oxide fracture and grain coarsening.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to conditions where the sliding contact is exposed to atmospheric oxygen (or controlled air environments) under moderate to high loads and sliding speeds; its effectiveness in significantly different environments (e.g., ultra-high vacuum or liquid lubricated conditions) remains to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) the baseline CoCrFeNi HEA and (2) a CoCrFeNi alloy doped with ~0.5 at.% W. Conduct systematic pin-on-disk sliding experiments over a temperature range from RT to 800 °C under identical loads and sliding speeds in air. Use high-resolution surface microscopy and topographical interferometry to assess wear track morphologies and measure friction coefficients as a function of temperature.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) at different temperatures
Surface microstructure and tribolayer characteristics (e.g., via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the W-doped alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate relative to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy under the full temperature range (RT to 800 °C), or if no stable adaptive tribolayer is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor alloying addition of tungsten to the CoCrFeNi matrix will promote the in‐situ formation of a stable, nanocomposite tribolayer that maintains low friction and low wear over the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
drafts.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with coarse-grained, single-phase FCC microstructure exhibiting relatively high friction and wear under variable temperature sliding conditions.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small (e.g., on the order of 0.5–1 at.%) tungsten addition into the CoCrFeNi alloy during processing.
drafts.conditions: Sliding friction tests conducted in air (or controlled environment) across a temperature range from RT to 800 °C under variable normal loads and sliding speeds.
drafts.structural_mediator: The tungsten segregates during deformation to stimulate dynamic nanograin refinement and precipitate (or intermetallic/oxide) formation at the sliding interface, which acts as a self-adaptive, lubricious tribolayer.
drafts.mechanism: W doping increases lattice distortion that enhances shear-induced grain refinement and promotes the formation of hard, yet adaptable, nanoprecipitates and/or oxide phases. At low temperatures, the refined nanostructure lowers interfacial shear strength, while at high temperatures, the tungsten-assisted formation of a protective glaze layer (or intermetallic/oxide) minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the tungsten-doped variant will show a lower and more stable friction coefficient (targeting values near or below ~0.2–0.3) and significantly reduced wear rates (by up to one order of magnitude) over the entire temperature interval.
drafts.baseline: The current CoCrFeNi alloy without tungsten, which suffers from rising wear or variable friction as temperature and loading conditions change.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under sliding conditions between room temperature and 800 °C in environments without excessive oxidation agents beyond ambient air; its performance under extreme loads or chemically aggressive atmospheres remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and another of CoCrFeNi alloy doped with ~0.5–1 at.% tungsten. Subject both to identical ball-on-disk sliding tests over a temperature range from RT to 800 °C under controlled normal loads and sliding speeds in air. Analyze the friction coefficients in real time and measure volume loss using interferometric profiling after testing.
measurements: Wear track dimension and specific wear rate (mm³/N·m)
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM/SEM) of the worn layer to identify nanograin refinement and secondary phase formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant and reproducible reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the undoped baseline — or if the wear layer does not show evidence of the predicted nanocomposite tribolayer — then the hypothesis is falsified.
